standard.title: Ideas, values and contexts in literary texts
standard.description: explain the ways that ideas and points of view may represent the values of individuals and groups in literary texts, drawn from historical, social and cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify how ideas and points of view in literary texts reflect social and cultural contexts, including First Nations Australian perspectives (AC9E7LE01). They have not yet explained how values are embedded in these representations or systematically connected contextual knowledge to meaning-making in texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how ideas and points of view in literary texts represent the values of individuals and groups in relation to their historical, social and cultural contexts, including texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Values embedded in representation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify ideas or points of view in a literary text and explain what values they reflect — including whose values and what context those values belong to.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one idea or point of view in a literary text and explain what values it reflects about the individual or group it represents, connecting those values to a specific historical, social or cultural context.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how ideas and points of view in a literary text represent the values of particular individuals or groups in their historical, social or cultural context; draw on contextual knowledge to explain why those values appear in the text.
wider: Explain how values represented in a text from a historical context (e.g. the romantic representation of the Australian swagman) differ from contemporary values about the same subject
Examine how a literary text by a First Nations Australian author represents values, ways of being and knowing that differ distinctly from mainstream Australian literary traditions
Compare how the same historical period is represented in texts from different cultural perspectives, examining whose values each text prioritises

response_modes.reason: The move from 'what ideas are in this text' to 'these ideas reflect these specific values from this context' requires explicit scaffolding. Students tend to make general contextual claims rather than grounding them in specific textual evidence. Structured reasoning support at this node builds the habit of linking textual detail to contextual claim.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of historical, social and cultural contexts available — from colonial Australian literature to contemporary First Nations writing to world literature from diverse traditions — provides rich comparative ground for exploring how values are contextually situated.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific idea or point of view in a text and names the values it reflects.
Connects those values to a specific historical, social or cultural context with reference to the text.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to explain how First Nations and diverse authors represent distinct values shaped by their cultural contexts — a move that depends on the conceptual scaffold built at Node 1 (linking textual evidence to contextual claim). Students who have not built this reasoning structure produce vague contextual claims at Node 2 rather than grounded textual explanation.

nodes.label: First Nations and diverse author perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how literary texts by First Nations Australian authors represent unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing, and how texts by wide-ranging Australian and world authors offer diverse perspectives shaped by their contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one text by a First Nations Australian or culturally diverse author represents a perspective or set of values shaped by the author's cultural context, identifying at least one specific way it differs from mainstream representations.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how texts by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors from a range of cultural contexts represent distinct values and perspectives; explain how these representations reflect the social and cultural contexts from which the texts emerge.
wider: Compare how two authors from different cultural backgrounds (e.g. a First Nations Australian and a British author) represent the natural world, examining what values about land, country and environment each text encodes
Investigate how a First Nations Australian text represents ways of being, knowing and doing that are absent from or marginalised in mainstream Australian literature
Examine how reading texts from unfamiliar cultural contexts challenges or expands a reader's own values and perspectives

response_modes.reason: Understanding that perspective is always culturally situated — and that different contexts produce genuinely different ways of understanding the world — requires exposure to texts from multiple diverse contexts. A single text cannot establish the comparative understanding the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Explains how a text by a First Nations Australian or diverse author represents a perspective or set of values shaped by a specific cultural context.
Identifies at least one specific way the representation differs from or challenges mainstream representations.
